subject: phoenix
pitch: A phoenix rising with its wings flung open. Feathers blaze from deep crimson at the body through orange to golden yellow at the tips, a crest of flame-shaped plumes on its head, long trailing tail feathers like ribbons of fire, glowing amber eyes and a golden hooked beak. Embers and sparks drift off its wings.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module using the SDK to model a phoenix with wings open in a rising pose, deciding whether it should appear lifted off the ground given the "rising" theme.

To reconcile the ground-contact rule with a flying pose, I'll add a small ember pyre or ash mound touching y=0 beneath the phoenix, letting the bird itself hover above it. I'm sketching proportions—roughly 1.6m wingspan, 0.8m body length, facing +Z—and starting to lay out the joint hierarchy with the root body positioned above the pyre.

Working out the spine chain...

Still defining sweep radius and gradient paints...

Defining wing gradients and feather geometry...

Still planning feather placement...

Adding wing joint names and planning the feather sweep along the wing chain, with primaries fanning out from the hand joint.

Still defining feather outline points...

For the feather coloring, I'm considering a gradient paint from root crimson to tip gold applied per feather, reusing the same gradient style for each since individual paints are cheap even though there will be several baked into the chart.

Now I'm sketching the eyes as small amber spheres, then the hooked beak as a tapering swept capsule following a curved path from the head out to a pointed tip. I'm also planning flame-shaped crest plumes on the head as tall vertical extruded outlines facing outward.

For the tail, I'm chaining joints trailing back and down from the pelvis, then building long ribbon-like extruded feathers along that path with thin lateral width, spaced across the tail base and sized so their tips stay above ground level.

For embers and sparks, I'm scattering small emissive spheres around the wings using randomized positions, maybe thirty of them. For the pyre, I'm building a lathe-shaped mound at the ground with layered cone-shaped flames rising from it, colored to suggest burning wood and fire.

The phoenix hovers above the flames rather than touching them, so I'm deciding whether to add tucked legs or skip them for simplicity, leaning toward brief capsule-shaped legs folded under the belly. For the head and neck, I'm extending the spine chain upward through chest and neck points into the head position to keep the body continuous.

I'm setting up the spine as a smooth chain with named joints ending in a head tip, then branching off separate chains for the tail and wings that attach near the nearest spine joint, with a mirrored wing function so both sides share geometry but flip across the x-axis.

Now I'm sweeping the body along the spine using an array of radii to shape it thin at the tail, bulky at the chest, narrowing at the neck, and widening slightly at the head, then applying a similar tapered sweep along the wing chain and planning flight feathers positioned along the outer portion of the wing.

I'm figuring out the orientation of each feather relative to the wing's flat horizontal plane: the feather's length direction points outward and slightly back, its width lies in-plane perpendicular to that direction, and its thickness extrudes along the vertical normal, so feathers sit flush like a flat fan over the wing surface.

For the mirrored side, I just flip the x-component of the direction vector and recompute the in-plane perpendicular, since the sign of the perpendicular doesn't matter — the thickness extrusion is symmetric either way, so the mesh looks correct regardless of winding.

Now I'm sketching a feather helper function that takes a position, a normalized direction, length, width, color, and bone, computes a perpendicular vector with a slight upward tilt, then extrudes a tapered feather-shaped outline along those axes with a small thickness value controlling how thick the feather blade is.

Planning out the wing feather layout now: primaries along the outer hand with longer, backward-angled feathers, secondaries closer to the body with a different angle, plus coverts, all positioned using joint references along the wing's bone chain from shoulder through elbow and wrist to the wingtip.

I'm setting up unique joint names for each wing segment so the chain renders correctly with catmull interpolation, and deciding to keep the legs simple with tucked talons. For coloring, I'm laying out gradients across the body, tail, and wings that transition from deep crimson at the base through orange to golden tips, giving the phoenix its fiery blaze effect.

Deciding against overly complex blended paints for the wings and just going with a clean two-tone gradient from deep red to golden-orange, skipping grain texture for simplicity. Now placing small amber sphere eyes near the head joint position.

Working out the beak as a hooked sweep with decreasing radius from base to tip, colored gold and bound to the head bone, then starting to sketch the head crest as a series of flame-shaped extruded outlines with sharp tips pointing upward and back.

I'm checking whether my flame polygon points create self-intersecting edges, adjusting the coordinates so the outline stays a valid simple polygon without crossing segments.

Now I'm working out placement for the crest plumes on top of the head, deciding to position several small plumes near the head joint with slight directional tilts rather than varying sizes, and figuring out which local axes (lateral vs. up-back) the extrusion should follow so the plume geometry orients correctly along the skull.

I'm also setting up the wing feather and tail ribbon geometry, defining the length and width directions for each extrusion, and sketching out a reusable ribbon/feather point generator so I can scale shapes consistently. For the tail, I'm working through the chain of spine points and checking how far a 1-meter ribbon extends along the tail's backward-curving direction from its base.

Next I'm positioning multiple ribbons across the tail with slight lateral offsets and matching angular tilts, and sharing a single crimson-to-gold gradient paint across them for efficiency. Then I'm moving on to building the pyre mound using a lathed profile and placing flame cones with warm orange and gold coloring around its base, anchoring each piece near the ground joint.

Now I'm scattering small ember spheres around the wingtips using a seeded random generator, keeping total part count well under budget alongside feathers, crest spikes, ribbons, and flame cones. I'm deciding to skip visible legs for simplicity, though I consider adding tucked talon capsules near the pyre top before reconsidering whether the floating phoenix even needs them given it's meant to be rising rather than standing.

Realizing I need a root joint before building the chain, I'm creating a "hips" joint at the base position so the spine chain's weight calculations have something to attach to, then mapping out five spine joint names across four catmull-spline spans from the five control points, working through how the uniform parameter spacing will place each joint along the curve.

For the tail and wing chains, I'm planning catmull splines with their own joint names and tip markers, each parented to whichever nearby joint (hips, spine, or shoulder) ends up closest to the chain's starting point. Then I'm thinking through sweeping the body mesh along the spine chain using a radius array matched across the chain's parameter range.

For the wings, I'm sweeping tapered radii along the wing chain and deriving feather placement from points along that same chain, using separate direction and sizing rules for primary feathers (further out, angled backward/outward, longer and narrower) versus secondary feathers (closer in, angled mostly backward, shorter and wider), with root positions offset slightly off the arm.

For coloring, I decide to reuse a single wing gradient paint (crimson to gold, root to tip) across all wing feathers rather than computing a unique gradient per feather, relying on the blend function clamping values beyond t=1 so feathers extending past the gradient's defined range still look fine. Now I'm setting up the module structure: importing the builder utilities, creating the phoenix build function that returns the root object, and defining the exported metadata.

Now I'm placing specific body parts: eye pupils as small dark spheres, joint definitions for hips and head with directional vectors, and a spine path built from catmull points with varying sweep radii from tail to head. I'm positioning the eyes on the head's surface based on its radius and tip location, then constructing the beak as a tapered sweep with its own radius profile and golden coloring.

Still writing crest plume geometry...

Positioning pyre cone flames around the ring with alternating colors, then generating scattered sparks rising from random points along both wings using randomized offsets and small sphere geometries for each.

I'm also sketching tucked legs using mirrored capsule shapes in a muted gold tone, double-checking that wing joint references and vector positions work correctly for attaching feather extrusions along the bone chain.

For the colors, I'm setting up gradients and custom paint functions—crimson-to-gold for the body, a separate gradient for the tail, and a position-based paint function for the wings that mixes colors based on distance from center so both sides look symmetric despite mirrored coordinates. I also work out the perpendicular vector math needed so wing feathers lie flat with horizontal width rather than standing up vertically.

Now I'm writing out the actual phoenix construction code: defining helper functions for feather/plume outline shapes, building the spine chain and body sweep, placing eyes and beak on the head bone, adding a crest of flame-like plumes, constructing the wing function with primary and secondary feathers, and building the tail chain with ribbon-like extrusions fanning out behind it...

Then I move to the pyre base—a lathed bowl shape with cone-shaped flames arranged in a ring plus a taller central flame—followed by simple capsule talons for the legs. I add a scattering of small spherical sparks positioned randomly along the wing arms using a seeded RNG, then close out by returning the root group, double-checking that all the bone assignments, sweep radii, and paint references are consistent throughout.
